title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

Formulate a vehicle routing problem as a mathematical model
Explain how subtours arise and how to prevent them
Assess why large instances are hard to solve exactly
Choose between exact methods and heuristics in practice

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Central Libraries

Question: Does anyone have an idea what a central library is?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Central Libraries

Book Delivery to Libraries in Germany
They supply all local libraries within the same state
Complex, as number of libraries per state can be large
Books and media in the libraries change often
Customers can request books from other libraries

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Structure of the Deliveries

For delivery, the central library has several employees and cars
Local libraries differ in size, some receive more items
Items are collected as well during the tours1
They are transported back to the central library

Due to regulations, the delivery tours cannot exceed a certain duration

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Potential Decisions
Question: What decisions can the library make for tours?


Subdivide set of libraries into several ordered tours
Decide in which order to visit the libraries
Evaluate which car to use for each of the tours
Decide which driver to assign to each of the tours

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Impact of the Decisions
Question: What is the impact of the decisions?


Longer driving increases the footprint of the deliveries
Suboptimal tours can lead to unnecessary costs
Fuel, personnel, and repairs are increased
Unhappy customers due to waiting times on books

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Have you heard of
this problem before?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Objective
Question: What could be the objective for central libraries?


Lowering costs through improved tours
Improvement of their footprint through shorter tours
Faster fulfillment of the deliveries

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Modelling
Question: What could we try to model?

Minimization of the travel time while supplying all libraries in the state and respecting the vehicle capacities and driving time restrictions.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Capacitated
Vehicle Routing
(CVRP)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Vehicle Routing Problem

CVRP is a subproblem
Main problem is Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP)
Problem class about designing routes for vehicle fleets








There are many variants of the VRP! E.g., with time windows, periodic deliveries, allowing for pickups or deliveries, and much more!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Let’s visualize
the problem!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Basic Problem Setting

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Basic Setting with Arcs

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Setting with Vehicles

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Basic Setting with Tours

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Available Sets
Question: What could be the sets here?


\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(\mathcal{A}\) - Set of all arcs between the nodes, index \((i,j) \in \mathcal{A}\)
\(\mathcal{K}\) - Set of vehicles with identical capacity, index \(k \in \mathcal{K}\)
\(0 \in \mathcal{V}\) - Depot where the vehicles start

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Available Parameters
Question: What are possible parameters?


\(b\) - Capacity per vehicle
\(t\) - Maximal duration of each tour
\(d_i\) - Demand at node \(i\)
\(c_{i,j}\) - Travel time on an arc from \(i\) to \(j\)









\(t\) is the maximal duration of each tour, not the travel time on an arc or an index!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Decision Variable(s)?






We have the following sets:



All nodes, including the depot, \(i \in \mathcal{V}\)
All arcs between the nodes, \((i,j) \in \mathcal{A}\)
The available vehicles, \(k \in \mathcal{K}\)











Our objective is to:


Minimize the total travel time while supplying all customers and adhering to the vehicle capacities and duration restrictions.





Question: What could be our decision variable/s?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Decision Variables

\(X_{i,j,k}\) - 1, if \(k\) passes between \(i\) and \(j\) on its tour, 0 otherwise








Variable Domain


\(X_{i,j,k}\) is a binary variable, as it can only take values 0 or 1. But most likely, you will already have spotted that!





Question: Why might this make the problem difficult?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Decision Variable/s (again)?






We have the following sets:



All nodes, including the depot, \(i \in \mathcal{V}\)
All arcs between the nodes, \((i,j) \in \mathcal{A}\)
The available vehicles, \(k \in \mathcal{K}\)











Our objective is to:


Minimization of the travel time (or driving distance), while supplying all customers and adhering to the vehicle capacities and duration restrictions. Hint: Even with many vehicles, each arc can maximally be passed once!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Decision Variables (again)
Question: What could be our decision variable/s?


\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, else 0









Only possible under certain conditions!


Only possible, if time and capacity constraints are equal for all vehicles!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Objective Function?






Our objective is to:


Minimization of the travel time (or driving distance), while supplying all customers and adhering to the vehicle capacities and duration restrictions.




Question: What could be our objective function?








We need the following variable:



\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, else 0

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Objective Function






We need the following parameters:



\(c_{i,j}\) - travel time on an arc from \(i\) to \(j\)





\[\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}\]


Question: What does \((i,j) \in \mathcal{A}\) under the sum mean?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
From Math to Code
The objective function in JuMP looks very similar:

using JuMP, HiGHS

# Simple example with 4 nodes
nodes = ["depot", "A", "B", "C"]
arcs = [(i,j) for i in nodes, j in nodes if i != j]
c = Dict(("depot","A") => 10, ("depot","B") => 15, ("depot","C") => 20,
         ("A","depot") => 10, ("A","B") => 12, ("A","C") => 8,
         ("B","depot") => 15, ("B","A") => 12, ("B","C") => 5,
         ("C","depot") => 20, ("C","A") => 8, ("C","B") => 5)

model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
@variable(model, X[arcs], Bin)
@objective(model, Min, sum(c[(i,j)] * X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs))








The JuMP syntax sum(c[(i,j)] * X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs) directly mirrors our mathematical notation \(\sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}\)!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Solving the Small Example
Let’s add constraints and solve the example with one vehicle:

# Each node has to be entered and left exactly once
for n in nodes
    @constraint(model, sum(X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs if j == n) == 1)
    @constraint(model, sum(X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs if i == n) == 1)
end
set_silent(model)
optimize!(model)
println("Arcs: ", [a for a in arcs if value(X[a]) > 0.5])
println("Cost: ", objective_value(model))

Arcs: [("A", "depot"), ("depot", "A"), ("C", "B"), ("B", "C")]
Cost: 30.0

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
A Valid Solution?
The solver chose the arcs depot ↔︎ A and B ↔︎ C with a cost of 30.

Question: Is this a valid tour for one vehicle?



No! The loop B ↔︎ C never visits the depot
Our model is still missing constraints
We will fix this in the following sections!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Problem Constraints

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Constraints?
Question: What constraints do we need?


Each customer has to be visited once
The depot has to be entered and left \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times
We have to enforce the capacity of our vehicles
We have to ensure the maximal duration of each tour









Subtours


In addition, we have to prevent subtours!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
What is a
subtour?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Subtours

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Visit Each Customer Once?






The goal of these constraints is to:


Ensure that each customer is visited exactly once. Essentially, we could also say that each node has to be entered and left exactly once.










We need the following sets and variables:



\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Visit Each Customer Once
Question: What could the constraint look like?

\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}, i \neq j} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}, j \neq i} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]


Question: Why for all nodes except the depot?


The depot is the only node that is visited multiple times!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot Entry/Exit Constraints?






The goal of these constraints is to:


Ensure that each vehicle enters and leaves the depot exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times, as we have \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles and each vehicle has to return to the depot.










We need the following sets and variables:



\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(|\mathcal{K}|\) - Number of vehicles
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise






Question: What could the constraint look like?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot Entry/Exit Constraints
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{i,0} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{0,j} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]







Are all constraints necessary?


No, theoretically we could also say that we only have to leave or enter the depot exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times, as the other constraint is already enforced by the “visit each customer once constraint”.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) Tours?
Question: What if 3 vehicles would suffice, but we own 5?


The constraints force all \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles to be used
With generous capacity, this can lead to more tours than needed and thus longer total travel times
Replacing \(=\) with \(\leq\) would allow the solver to leave vehicles unused

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
The next ones are
a little bit tricky.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
MTZ Formulation

Miller-Tucker-Zemlin (MTZ) Constraints from 1960
Here, in the CVRP form of Kara et al. (2004)
Prevent subtours and track routes and capacity utilization
First, we need an additional variable!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
The MTZ Variable

\(U_{i}\) - Capacity utilization at \(i\) of vehicle on its tour with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
Note that \(U_i\) is a continuous variable, not a binary one!








You don’t need to guess these constraints, as they are quite tricky!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
MTZ Constraints






We need the following sets, parameters, and variables:



\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise
\(U_{i}\) - Capacity utilization at \(i\) of vehicle on its tour with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(b\) - Capacity per vehicle (all are identical!)
\(d_i\) - Demand at node \(i\)





\[
U_i - U_j + b \times X_{i,j} \leq b - d_j \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]


\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Too
complicated?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Don’t worry!





Let’s break it down!
\(d_i\) for all customers is 1
Capacity \(b\) per vehicle is 5
\(U_i\) is the current capacity utilization at node \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
No connection between nodes





In case \(X_{i,j} = 0\):

\(U_i - U_j \leq b - d_j\)
Non-binding for relation between two nodes

Following is perfectly fine:

\(U_i \leq b\) and \(U_j \geq d_j\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Connection between two nodes





In case \(X_{i,j} = 1\):

\[U_i - U_j + b \leq b - d_j\]
Binding for relation between two nodes

Can be summarized to:

\(U_j \geq d_j + U_i\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Connection in more detail
Question: Why is it binding?


Binding as \(U_j\) has to be at least as large as \(d_j + U_i\)
Hence, fulfilled if the demand of \(j\) is added to the vehicle



Question: Do you get the idea?



If \(X_{i,j} = 1\), then \(U_j\) has to be at least as large as \(d_j + U_i\)
If \(X_{i,j} = 0\), then \(U_i \leq b\) and \(U_j \geq d_j\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour from the Depot





Tour of vehicle A ok
Depot is the only node visited multiple times
But the constraints are not applied here!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own





Assume a subtour \(H \to C \to I \to H\)
Each arc on it has \(X_{i,j} = 1\)
From \(H\) to \(C\):
\(U_C \geq U_H + 1\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own II





From \(C\) to \(I\):
\(U_I \geq U_C + 1\)
\(U\) has to increase along every arc of the subtour

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own III





From \(I\) back to \(H\):
\(U_H \geq U_I + 1\)
Now, add up all three constraints
All \(U\) cancel out: \(0 \geq 3\)
Impossible! No feasible values for \(U\) exist!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Subtour Elimination

The same argument holds for any subtour without the depot
Only depot as “reset”, as constraints are not applied here

Question: What about the capacity?


Remember variable domain of \(U_i\)?
\(d_i \leq U_i \leq b\) → Overall capacity limit enforced!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Ensure time limit?
Question: Does anyone have an idea?


Constraints basically follow the same idea!
First, we again need an additional variable
\(T_{i}\) - Time spent on tour at node \(i\) of a vehicle with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(T_i\) is a continuous variable, just like \(U_i\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Ensure time limit






We need the following sets and variables:



\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise
\(T_{i}\) - Time spent on tour at the node \(i\) of a vehicle with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(t\) - Maximal duration of a tour
\(c_{i,j}\) - Travel time on an arc from \(i\) to \(j\)





\[
T_i - T_j + t \times X_{i,j} \leq t - c_{i,j} \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]


\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_{i} \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Time limit and the depot
Question: Why do we need the tightened domain of \(T_i\)?


\(T_i \geq c_{0,i}\): the drive from the depot to the first customer counts
\(T_i \leq t - c_{i,0}\): time to return to the depot is reserved
With just \(0 \leq T_i \leq t\), a tour could exceed the limit by the two depot legs!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Any questions?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Objective
\[
\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}
\]






The goal of the objective function is to:


Minimize the total travel distance.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Each customer is visited once
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}, i \neq j} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}, j \neq i} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






Our constraints ensure:


Each customer is visited exactly once.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot entry and exit
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{i,0} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{0,j} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]






Our constraints ensure:


The depot is visited by exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles. Note, that we could remove one of the constraints and the solution would still be optimal.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Capacity/subtour elimination
\[
U_i - U_j + b \times X_{i,j} \leq b - d_j \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






Our constraints ensure:


The capacity limit is respected and subtours are eliminated.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Time constraints
\[
T_i - T_j + t \times X_{i,j} \leq t - c_{i,j} \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_i \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






Our constraints ensure:


The time limit is respected (and subtours are eliminated). The domain of \(T_i\) accounts for the travel from and back to the depot.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Variables
\[
X_{i,j} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}
\]
\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_i \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






The variable domains make sure that:


The binary setup variable is either 0 or 1 and the continuous variables \(U_i\) and \(T_i\) stay within the capacity and time limits.

We have already encountered NP-hard problems in this course

The CVRP is a generalization of the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), which is itself NP-hard!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Understanding Optimality Gap

The optimality gap measures: \[\frac{\text{Best Solution} - \text{Lower Bound}}{\text{Lower Bound}} \times 100\%\]
A 40% gap means our solution could be up to 40% worse than optimal1

Note that most solvers (including HiGHS) report the gap relative to the best solution, \(\frac{\text{Best Solution} - \text{Lower Bound}}{\text{Best Solution}}\), so the numbers in the solver log differ slightly from our definition.

For 165 libraries, even state-of-the-art solvers struggle



This is why we need heuristics!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
From Math to Code
The objective function in JuMP looks very similar:

using JuMP, HiGHS

# Simple example with 4 nodes
nodes = ["depot", "A", "B", "C"]
arcs = [(i,j) for i in nodes, j in nodes if i != j]
c = Dict(("depot","A") => 10, ("depot","B") => 15, ("depot","C") => 20,
         ("A","depot") => 10, ("A","B") => 12, ("A","C") => 8,
         ("B","depot") => 15, ("B","A") => 12, ("B","C") => 5,
         ("C","depot") => 20, ("C","A") => 8, ("C","B") => 5)

model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
@variable(model, X[arcs], Bin)
@objective(model, Min, sum(c[(i,j)] * X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs))

. . .






The JuMP syntax sum(c[(i,j)] * X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs) directly mirrors our mathematical notation \(\sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}\)!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Solving the Small Example
Let’s add constraints and solve the example with one vehicle:

# Each node has to be entered and left exactly once
for n in nodes
    @constraint(model, sum(X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs if j == n) == 1)
    @constraint(model, sum(X[(i,j)] for (i,j) in arcs if i == n) == 1)
end
set_silent(model)
optimize!(model)
println("Arcs: ", [a for a in arcs if value(X[a]) > 0.5])
println("Cost: ", objective_value(model))

Arcs: [("A", "depot"), ("depot", "A"), ("C", "B"), ("B", "C")]
Cost: 30.0

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
A Valid Solution?
The solver chose the arcs depot ↔︎ A and B ↔︎ C with a cost of 30.
. . .
Question: Is this a valid tour for one vehicle?
. . .

No! The loop B ↔︎ C never visits the depot
Our model is still missing constraints
We will fix this in the following sections!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Problem Constraints

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Constraints?
Question: What constraints do we need?
. . .

Each customer has to be visited once
The depot has to be entered and left \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times
We have to enforce the capacity of our vehicles
We have to ensure the maximal duration of each tour

. . .






ImportantSubtours



In addition, we have to prevent subtours!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
What is a
subtour?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Subtours

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Visit Each Customer Once?






ImportantThe goal of these constraints is to:



Ensure that each customer is visited exactly once. Essentially, we could also say that each node has to be entered and left exactly once.


. . .






NoteWe need the following sets and variables:




\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Visit Each Customer Once
Question: What could the constraint look like?
. . .
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}, i \neq j} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}, j \neq i} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
. . .
Question: Why for all nodes except the depot?
. . .
The depot is the only node that is visited multiple times!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot Entry/Exit Constraints?






ImportantThe goal of these constraints is to:



Ensure that each vehicle enters and leaves the depot exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times, as we have \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles and each vehicle has to return to the depot.


. . .






NoteWe need the following sets and variables:




\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(|\mathcal{K}|\) - Number of vehicles
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise



. . .
Question: What could the constraint look like?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot Entry/Exit Constraints
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{i,0} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{0,j} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]
. . .






NoteAre all constraints necessary?



No, theoretically we could also say that we only have to leave or enter the depot exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) times, as the other constraint is already enforced by the “visit each customer once constraint”.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) Tours?
Question: What if 3 vehicles would suffice, but we own 5?
. . .

The constraints force all \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles to be used
With generous capacity, this can lead to more tours than needed and thus longer total travel times
Replacing \(=\) with \(\leq\) would allow the solver to leave vehicles unused

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
The next ones are
a little bit tricky.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
MTZ Formulation


Miller-Tucker-Zemlin (MTZ) Constraints from 1960
Here, in the CVRP form of Kara et al. (2004)
Prevent subtours and track routes and capacity utilization
First, we need an additional variable!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
The MTZ Variable

\(U_{i}\) - Capacity utilization at \(i\) of vehicle on its tour with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
Note that \(U_i\) is a continuous variable, not a binary one!

. . .






You don’t need to guess these constraints, as they are quite tricky!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
MTZ Constraints






NoteWe need the following sets, parameters, and variables:




\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise
\(U_{i}\) - Capacity utilization at \(i\) of vehicle on its tour with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(b\) - Capacity per vehicle (all are identical!)
\(d_i\) - Demand at node \(i\)



. . .
\[
U_i - U_j + b \times X_{i,j} \leq b - d_j \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
. . .
\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Too
complicated?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Don’t worry!





Let’s break it down!
\(d_i\) for all customers is 1
Capacity \(b\) per vehicle is 5
\(U_i\) is the current capacity utilization at node \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
No connection between nodes





In case \(X_{i,j} = 0\):

\(U_i - U_j \leq b - d_j\)
Non-binding for relation between two nodes

Following is perfectly fine:

\(U_i \leq b\) and \(U_j \geq d_j\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Connection between two nodes





In case \(X_{i,j} = 1\):

\[U_i - U_j + b \leq b - d_j\]
Binding for relation between two nodes

Can be summarized to:

\(U_j \geq d_j + U_i\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Connection in more detail
Question: Why is it binding?
. . .

Binding as \(U_j\) has to be at least as large as \(d_j + U_i\)
Hence, fulfilled if the demand of \(j\) is added to the vehicle

. . .
Question: Do you get the idea?
. . .

If \(X_{i,j} = 1\), then \(U_j\) has to be at least as large as \(d_j + U_i\)
If \(X_{i,j} = 0\), then \(U_i \leq b\) and \(U_j \geq d_j\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour from the Depot





Tour of vehicle A ok
Depot is the only node visited multiple times
But the constraints are not applied here!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own





Assume a subtour \(H \to C \to I \to H\)
Each arc on it has \(X_{i,j} = 1\)
From \(H\) to \(C\):
\(U_C \geq U_H + 1\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own II





From \(C\) to \(I\):
\(U_I \geq U_C + 1\)
\(U\) has to increase along every arc of the subtour

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Tour on its Own III





From \(I\) back to \(H\):
\(U_H \geq U_I + 1\)
Now, add up all three constraints
All \(U\) cancel out: \(0 \geq 3\)
Impossible! No feasible values for \(U\) exist!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Subtour Elimination

The same argument holds for any subtour without the depot
Only depot as “reset”, as constraints are not applied here

Question: What about the capacity?
. . .

Remember variable domain of \(U_i\)?
\(d_i \leq U_i \leq b\) → Overall capacity limit enforced!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Ensure time limit?
Question: Does anyone have an idea?
. . .

Constraints basically follow the same idea!
First, we again need an additional variable
\(T_{i}\) - Time spent on tour at node \(i\) of a vehicle with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(T_i\) is a continuous variable, just like \(U_i\)

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Ensure time limit






NoteWe need the following sets and variables:




\(\mathcal{V}\) - Set of all nodes, index \(i \in \{0,1,2,...,n\}\)
\(X_{i,j}\) - 1, if the arc between \(i\) and \(j\) is part of a tour, 0 otherwise
\(T_{i}\) - Time spent on tour at the node \(i\) of a vehicle with \(i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}\)
\(t\) - Maximal duration of a tour
\(c_{i,j}\) - Travel time on an arc from \(i\) to \(j\)



. . .
\[
T_i - T_j + t \times X_{i,j} \leq t - c_{i,j} \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
. . .
\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_{i} \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Time limit and the depot
Question: Why do we need the tightened domain of \(T_i\)?
. . .

\(T_i \geq c_{0,i}\): the drive from the depot to the first customer counts
\(T_i \leq t - c_{i,0}\): time to return to the depot is reserved
With just \(0 \leq T_i \leq t\), a tour could exceed the limit by the two depot legs!

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text: Any questions?

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Objective
\[
\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}
\]






ImportantThe goal of the objective function is to:



Minimize the total travel distance.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Each customer is visited once
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}, i \neq j} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}, j \neq i} X_{i,j} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






ImportantOur constraints ensure:



Each customer is visited exactly once.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Depot entry and exit
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{i,0} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}} X_{0,j} = |\mathcal{K}|
\]






ImportantOur constraints ensure:



The depot is visited by exactly \(|\mathcal{K}|\) vehicles. Note, that we could remove one of the constraints and the solution would still be optimal.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Capacity/subtour elimination
\[
U_i - U_j + b \times X_{i,j} \leq b - d_j \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






ImportantOur constraints ensure:



The capacity limit is respected and subtours are eliminated.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Time constraints
\[
T_i - T_j + t \times X_{i,j} \leq t - c_{i,j} \quad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}, i \neq j
\]
\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_i \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






ImportantOur constraints ensure:



The time limit is respected (and subtours are eliminated). The domain of \(T_i\) accounts for the travel from and back to the depot.

title: Lecture VII - Library Routing Optimization
text:
Variables
\[
X_{i,j} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}
\]
\[
d_i \leq U_i \leq b \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]
\[
c_{0,i} \leq T_i \leq t - c_{i,0} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{0\}
\]






ImportantThe variable domains make sure that:



The binary setup variable is either 0 or 1 and the continuous variables \(U_i\) and \(T_i\) stay within the capacity and time limits.

The optimality gap measures: \[\frac{\text{Best Solution} - \text{Lower Bound}}{\text{Lower Bound}} \times 100\%\]
A 40% gap means our solution could be up to 40% worse than optimal2

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Case Study





Large brewery
Brews and sells beverages
Production planning by hand
Planner has a lot of experience
But will retire soon

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Challenges





Strong competition
Customer demand is changing
Craft beer gains popularity
Variety of drinks is increasing
Batch sizes are getting smaller

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Different costs





Plant can fill multiple types
Time depends on type and batch
Changing type leads to setup costs for preparation and cleaning
Unsold beer bottles can be stored in a warehouse
This leads to inventory costs

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Learning Objectives
After this lecture, you will be able to:

Formulate the Capacitated Lot-Sizing Problem (CLSP)
Explain the trade-off between setup and inventory holding costs
Recognize and construct Big-M constraints
Discuss the assumptions and limits of a finite planning horizon

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Where is the
challenge?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective




Question: What could be the objective?
Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Trade-Off




Question: What is the trade-off?
Larger batches require less setup cost per bottle, but increase the storage cost.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Available Sets
Question: What are sets again?

Sets are collections of objects.


Question: What could be the sets here?



\(\mathcal{I}\) - Set of beer types indexed by \(i \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{I}|\}\)
\(\mathcal{T}\) - Set of time periods indexed by \(t \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{T}|\}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Available Parameters
Question: What are possible parameters?


\(a_t\) - Available time on the bottling plant in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(b_i\) - Time used for bottling one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(g_i\) - Setup time for beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(f_i\) - Setup cost of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(c_i\) - Inventory holding cost for one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Decision Variables?






We have the following sets:



Beer types indexed by \(i \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{I}|\}\)
Time periods of the planning horizon indexed by \(t \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{T}|\}\)











Our objective is to:


Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.





Question: What could be our decision variable/s?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Decision Variables

\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective Function?






Our objective is to:


Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.




Question: What could be our objective function?








We need the following variables:



\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective Function






We need the following parameters:



\(f_i\) - Setup cost of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(c_i\) - Inventory holding cost for one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)





\[\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} (c_i \times W_{i,t} + f_i \times Y_{i,t})\]

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Constraints




Question: What constraints?


Transfer unused inventory
Fulfill the customer demand
Set up beer types
Calculate batch size per set-up
Compute remaining inventory
Limit the bottling plant

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Demand/Inventory Constraints?






The goal of these constraints is to:


Consider the current inventory and batch sizes and compute the remaining inventory.










We need the following variables and parameters:



\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)






Question: What could the constraint look like?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Demand/Inventory Constraints
\[W_{i,t-1} + X_{i,t} - W_{i,t} = d_{i,t} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]
with \(W_{i,0} = 0\), as the warehouse starts empty.







Remember, these are the variables and parameters:



\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Why Fix the Starting Inventory?
Question: Why do we have to fix \(W_{i,0} = 0\)?

Otherwise, the solver could invent free starting inventory and would never need to bottle anything for the first weeks!

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Setup Constraints?






The goal of these constraints is to:


Set up beer types in all periods where the batch size is \(>\) 0.










We need the following variables and parameters:



\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)






Question: What could the second constraint be?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Setup Constraints
\[X_{i,t} \leq Y_{i,t} \times \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]

Question: Do you know this type of constraint?


This type of constraint is called a “Big-M” constraint!



M (here \(\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau}\)) is a large number
It is coupled with a binary variable (here \(Y_{i,t}\))
Like an if-then constraint

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Capacity Constraints?






The goal of these constraints is to:


Limit the capacity of the bottling plant per period.










We need the following variables and parameters:



\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(a_t\) - Available time on the bottling plant in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(b_i\) - Time used for bottling one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(g_i\) - Setup time for beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Capacity Constraints
Question: What could the third constraint be?
It uses more parameters than the previous constraints, but it is easier to understand.

\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (b_i \times X_{i,t} + g_i \times Y_{i,t}) \leq a_t \quad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\]


And that’s basically it!

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Objective Function
The complete model is known as the Capacitated Lot-Sizing Problem (CLSP).
\[\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} (c_i \times W_{i,t} + f_i \times Y_{i,t})\]






The goal of the objective function is to:


Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Constraints
\[W_{i,t-1} + X_{i,t} - W_{i,t} = d_{i,t} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T} \quad (W_{i,0} = 0)\]
\[X_{i,t} \leq Y_{i,t} \times \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]
\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (b_i \times X_{i,t} + g_i \times Y_{i,t}) \leq a_t \quad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\]






Our constraints ensure:


Demand is met, inventory transferred, setup taken care of, and capacity respected.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Variable Domains
\[Y_{i,t}\in\{0,1\} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I},t\in\mathcal{T}\]
\[W_{i,t}, X_{i,t}\geq 0 \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I},t\in\mathcal{T}\]






The variable domains make sure that:


The binary setup variable is either 0 or 1 and that the inventory and batch size are non-negative.




Question: Why is a continuous batch size acceptable here?


At this scale, rounding a batch of thousands of bottles changes the cost only marginally.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Variables in Julia
Question: How could we formulate the variables in Julia?


using JuMP, HiGHS
beer_types = ["IPA", "Lager", "Stout"] # Beer types
periods = 1:3 # Time periods (weeks)
clsp_model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
set_silent(clsp_model) # Hide the solver output




@variable(clsp_model, Y[i in beer_types, t in periods], Bin)
@variable(clsp_model, X[i in beer_types, t in periods] >= 0)
@variable(clsp_model, W[i in beer_types, t in 0:last(periods)] >= 0)



2-dimensional DenseAxisArray{JuMP.VariableRef,2,...} with index sets:
    Dimension 1, ["IPA", "Lager", "Stout"]
    Dimension 2, 0:3
And data, a 3×4 Matrix{JuMP.VariableRef}:
 W[IPA,0]    W[IPA,1]    W[IPA,2]    W[IPA,3]
 W[Lager,0]  W[Lager,1]  W[Lager,2]  W[Lager,3]
 W[Stout,0]  W[Stout,1]  W[Stout,2]  W[Stout,3]




Note, how we declare the inventory \(W\) also for period 0!

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries

Tightening the Big-M
Question: How small can we make M without cutting off solutions?


Production in period \(t\) only serves demand from \(t\) onward: \(M_{i,t} = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T} | \tau \geq t} d_{i,\tau}\)
Capacity limits a batch as well: \(M_{i,t} = (a_t - g_i)/b_i\)



The smaller of the two is the tighter bound — and tighter formulations are usually solved faster!

End-of-horizon effect


The model plans no inventory for demand after week \(|\mathcal{T}|\), as it does not know about it. In practice, this is solved by re-planning on a rolling horizon.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective




Question: What could be the objective?
Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Trade-Off




Question: What is the trade-off?
Larger batches require less setup cost per bottle, but increase the storage cost.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Available Sets
Question: What are sets again?
. . .
Sets are collections of objects.
. . .
Question: What could be the sets here?
. . .

\(\mathcal{I}\) - Set of beer types indexed by \(i \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{I}|\}\)
\(\mathcal{T}\) - Set of time periods indexed by \(t \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{T}|\}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Available Parameters
Question: What are possible parameters?
. . .

\(a_t\) - Available time on the bottling plant in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(b_i\) - Time used for bottling one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(g_i\) - Setup time for beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(f_i\) - Setup cost of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(c_i\) - Inventory holding cost for one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Decision Variables?






NoteWe have the following sets:




Beer types indexed by \(i \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{I}|\}\)
Time periods of the planning horizon indexed by \(t \in \{1,2,...,|\mathcal{T}|\}\)



. . .






ImportantOur objective is to:



Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.


. . .
Question: What could be our decision variable/s?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Decision Variables

\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective Function?






ImportantOur objective is to:



Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.


. . .
Question: What could be our objective function?
. . .






NoteWe need the following variables:




\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Objective Function






NoteWe need the following parameters:




\(f_i\) - Setup cost of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(c_i\) - Inventory holding cost for one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)



. . .
\[\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} (c_i \times W_{i,t} + f_i \times Y_{i,t})\]

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Constraints




Question: What constraints?


Transfer unused inventory
Fulfill the customer demand
Set up beer types
Calculate batch size per set-up
Compute remaining inventory
Limit the bottling plant

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Demand/Inventory Constraints?






ImportantThe goal of these constraints is to:



Consider the current inventory and batch sizes and compute the remaining inventory.


. . .






NoteWe need the following variables and parameters:




\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)



. . .
Question: What could the constraint look like?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Demand/Inventory Constraints
\[W_{i,t-1} + X_{i,t} - W_{i,t} = d_{i,t} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]
with \(W_{i,0} = 0\), as the warehouse starts empty.
. . .






NoteRemember, these are the variables and parameters:




\(W_{i,t}\) - Inventory of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) at the end of period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Why Fix the Starting Inventory?
Question: Why do we have to fix \(W_{i,0} = 0\)?
. . .
Otherwise, the solver could invent free starting inventory and would never need to bottle anything for the first weeks!

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Setup Constraints?






ImportantThe goal of these constraints is to:



Set up beer types in all periods where the batch size is \(>\) 0.


. . .






NoteWe need the following variables and parameters:




\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(d_{i,t}\) - Demand of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)



. . .
Question: What could the second constraint be?

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Setup Constraints
\[X_{i,t} \leq Y_{i,t} \times \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]
. . .
Question: Do you know this type of constraint?
. . .
This type of constraint is called a “Big-M” constraint!
. . .

M (here \(\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau}\)) is a large number
It is coupled with a binary variable (here \(Y_{i,t}\))
Like an if-then constraint

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Capacity Constraints?






ImportantThe goal of these constraints is to:



Limit the capacity of the bottling plant per period.


. . .






NoteWe need the following variables and parameters:




\(Y_{i,t}\) - 1, if beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) is bottled in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\), 0 otherwise
\(X_{i,t}\) - Batch size of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) in \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(a_t\) - Available time on the bottling plant in period \(t\in\mathcal{T}\)
\(b_i\) - Time used for bottling one unit of beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)
\(g_i\) - Setup time for beer type \(i\in\mathcal{I}\)

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Capacity Constraints
Question: What could the third constraint be?
It uses more parameters than the previous constraints, but it is easier to understand.
. . .
\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (b_i \times X_{i,t} + g_i \times Y_{i,t}) \leq a_t \quad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\]
. . .
And that’s basically it!

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Objective Function
The complete model is known as the Capacitated Lot-Sizing Problem (CLSP).
\[\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} (c_i \times W_{i,t} + f_i \times Y_{i,t})\]






ImportantThe goal of the objective function is to:



Minimize the combined setup and inventory holding cost while satisfying the demand and adhering to the production capacity.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Constraints
\[W_{i,t-1} + X_{i,t} - W_{i,t} = d_{i,t} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T} \quad (W_{i,0} = 0)\]
\[X_{i,t} \leq Y_{i,t} \times \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} d_{i,\tau} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I}, t\in\mathcal{T}\]
\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (b_i \times X_{i,t} + g_i \times Y_{i,t}) \leq a_t \quad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\]






ImportantOur constraints ensure:



Demand is met, inventory transferred, setup taken care of, and capacity respected.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
CLSP: Variable Domains
\[Y_{i,t}\in\{0,1\} \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I},t\in\mathcal{T}\]
\[W_{i,t}, X_{i,t}\geq 0 \quad \forall i\in\mathcal{I},t\in\mathcal{T}\]






ImportantThe variable domains make sure that:



The binary setup variable is either 0 or 1 and that the inventory and batch size are non-negative.


. . .
Question: Why is a continuous batch size acceptable here?
. . .
At this scale, rounding a batch of thousands of bottles changes the cost only marginally.

title: Lecture V - Planning in Breweries
text:
Variables in Julia
Question: How could we formulate the variables in Julia?
. . .

using JuMP, HiGHS
beer_types = ["IPA", "Lager", "Stout"] # Beer types
periods = 1:3 # Time periods (weeks)
clsp_model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
set_silent(clsp_model) # Hide the solver output

. . .

@variable(clsp_model, Y[i in beer_types, t in periods], Bin)
@variable(clsp_model, X[i in beer_types, t in periods] >= 0)
@variable(clsp_model, W[i in beer_types, t in 0:last(periods)] >= 0)

2-dimensional DenseAxisArray{JuMP.VariableRef,2,...} with index sets:
    Dimension 1, ["IPA", "Lager", "Stout"]
    Dimension 2, 0:3
And data, a 3×4 Matrix{JuMP.VariableRef}:
 W[IPA,0]    W[IPA,1]    W[IPA,2]    W[IPA,3]
 W[Lager,0]  W[Lager,1]  W[Lager,2]  W[Lager,3]
 W[Stout,0]  W[Stout,1]  W[Stout,2]  W[Stout,3]


. . .
Note, how we declare the inventory \(W\) also for period 0!

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Variables and Data Types

Variables are used to store values
Assign a value to a variable using the = operator
You can use different data types for variables
You can change the value of a variable








You can use the typeof function to check the type of a variable.

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Vectors and Matrices

Vectors and matrices are used to store multiple values
You can create them using the [ and ] operators
Access their elements using square brackets








You can use the push! function to add elements to a vector or the pop! function to remove elements from a vector.

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Comparisons and Logic

Comparisons are used to compare values
== checks if two values are equal
!= checks if two values are not equal
< and > check if one value is smaller or greater than the other
<= and >= also allow the two values to be equal
&& is true if both conditions are true
|| is true if at least one of two conditions is true

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Loops

Loops are used to repeat code
for loop repeats code for a fixed number of times
while loop repeats code as long as a condition is true



for product in ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
    println("We sell: $product")
end



We sell: apple
We sell: banana
We sell: cherry

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Conditionals

Conditionals run code only under certain conditions
if executes code if a condition is true
elseif checks a further condition if the previous one was false
else executes code if none of the conditions were true








Conditionals are not loops: they decide whether code runs, while loops decide how often it runs.

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Dictionaries

Dictionaries store key-value pairs, like a lookup table
Access a value by its key using square brackets
keys and values return all keys and values



student_ids = Dict("Elio" => 1001, "Bob" => 1002)
println("Elio's ID: ", student_ids["Elio"])



Elio's ID: 1001










Later in the course, we will use dictionaries to store and look up the data of our optimization models.

Variables are used to store values

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Vectors and matrices are used to store multiple values
You can create them using the [ and ] operators
Access their elements using square brackets

. . .






You can use the push! function to add elements to a vector or the pop! function to remove elements from a vector.

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Comparisons are used to compare values
== checks if two values are equal
!= checks if two values are not equal
< and > check if one value is smaller or greater than the other
<= and >= also allow the two values to be equal
&& is true if both conditions are true
|| is true if at least one of two conditions is true

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Loops are used to repeat code
for loop repeats code for a fixed number of times
while loop repeats code as long as a condition is true

. . .

for product in ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
    println("We sell: $product")
end

We sell: apple
We sell: banana
We sell: cherry

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Conditionals run code only under certain conditions
if executes code if a condition is true
elseif checks a further condition if the previous one was false
else executes code if none of the conditions were true

. . .






Conditionals are not loops: they decide whether code runs, while loops decide how often it runs.

title: Lecture III - Packages and Data Management
text:
Dictionaries store key-value pairs, like a lookup table
Access a value by its key using square brackets
keys and values return all keys and values

. . .

student_ids = Dict("Elio" => 1001, "Bob" => 1002)
println("Elio's ID: ", student_ids["Elio"])

Elio's ID: 1001

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What is algebraic modeling?

A “mathematical language” for optimization problems
Allows for describing complex systems and constraints
Based on linear algebra (Equations and Inequalities)

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
How to learn algebraic modeling?

Practice, practice, and practice!
Understand standard models and their approach
Develop an understanding of constraints
Understand the structure of a model’s solution space
Use available algorithms to determine solutions

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Central Questions

What is to be decided?
What is relevant to the decision?
What information is given and relevant?
What parameters (data) are needed?
Which variables and of which type are needed?








Modeling is a creative process!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Model Components

Sets
Parameters
Decision variables
Objective function
Constraints








We will go through these components step by step in each lecture!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Linear Optimization Model


Basic Model Formulation
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Maximize} \quad F = \sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}} c_j \times X_j
\end{aligned}
\]
subject to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}} a_{i,j} \times X_j  \le b_i && \forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&X_j \ge 0 &&  \forall  j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]

Model Components
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{I} &: \text{set of resources, indexed by } i,\\
\mathcal{J} &: \text{set of activities, indexed by } j,\\
F   &: \text{Objective function variable,}\\
X_{j}   &: \text{decision variables,}\\
c_{j}   &: \text{objective function coefficients,}\\
a_{i,j} &: \text{parameters,}\\
b_{i}   &: \text{parameters}
\end{aligned}
\]


Question: Have you ever seen something like this before?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What is this good for?

Good Question! A lot of things:

Modeling real-world problems
Solving complex systems
Optimizing resource allocation
Decision-making under constraints
Simulation and prediction

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
From Abstract to Concrete
We’ve just seen the general structure:

Sets (\(\mathcal{I}\), \(\mathcal{J}\))
Parameters (\(c_j\), \(a_{i,j}\), \(b_i\))
Decision variables (\(X_j\))
Objective function and constraints


Now let’s see how this works with a real problem!








Watch for these components as we build our first model together.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Description
A company is producing solar panels in Dresden and Laupheim and has to transport them to new solar farms near Hamburg, Munich, and Berlin. The quantities offered and demanded (truckloads) and the transport costs per truckload in Euro are summarized in the following table.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Transport Costs



Origin/Destination
Hamburg
Munich
Berlin
Available




Dresden
5010
4640

21

Example: A truckload from Dresden \(i=1\) to Munich \(j=2\) costs \(c_{1,2}=4640\) Euro. Moreover, it is necessary to fulfil all customer demands, as the contract has been signed.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text: Graphical Illustration

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What are we trying?
First, we always need to understand the objectives.

Question: What are our possible objectives?
Minimizing the transport costs over all truckloads while meeting the demand within the available supply.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Let’s break it down
step by step!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Sets
Remember, sets are collections of elements

Question: What sets are needed?


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{I} &: \text{Set of production sites, indexed by } i \text{ with } i \in \{1, \ldots, |\mathcal{I}|\}, \\
\mathcal{J} &: \text{Set of customers, indexed by } j \text{ with } j \in \{1, \ldots, |\mathcal{J}|\}.
\end{aligned}
\]








We often use plural names for sets and a calligraphic letter, e.g., \(\mathcal{I}\) and \(\mathcal{J}\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Parameters
Parameters are fixed values that are given.

Question: What parameters are needed?


\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{i,j} &: \text{Costs per truck load for transport from } i \text{ to } j, \\
a_i &: \text{Available truck loads at } i, \\
b_j &: \text{Customer demands at } j.
\end{aligned}
\]








We usually use the corresponding lower-case letter, e.g., \(c\), \(a\), and \(b\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Decision Variable

Decision variables are the values we are trying to find
Here, our objective is to minimize the transport costs


Question: What decision variables are needed?


\[
X_{i,j} : \text{Trucks that deliver panels from site } i \text{ to customer } j.
\]








We use upper-case letters to distinguish variables from parameters, e.g., \(X\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
These are our
building blocks!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Objective Function

The objective function is the value we are trying to minimize (or maximize)
Formalized as a sum of decision variables and parameters


Question: Do you remember the objective?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Minimizing the Transport Costs
Minimize the transport costs over all truckloads while meeting customer demand within the available supply from production sites.

Question: How can we write this down?


\[
\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Constraints

Constraints are conditions that must be met
They limit the solution space!

Question: Objective value without the supply and demand constraints?


The value is zero
Cheapest option: we simply transport nothing at all!



Question: What constraints are needed?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Supply Constraints
Ensure that the number of panels transported from a location does not exceed the available panels.

Question: How can we formalize this?


\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Demand Constraints
Ensure that the demand of each customer is covered.

Question: Any ideas?


\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Non-negativity Constraints
Ensure no negative number of truckloads are transported.

Question: Does anyone have an idea how to write this down?


\[
X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Transport Problem
The complete model can then be written as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Minimize} \quad F &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j} \\
\text{subject to:} \quad
&\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad &&\forall j \in \mathcal{J} \\
&X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Inequality Constraints
Question: Could we replace \(=\) by \(\geq\) in the demand constraint?


Yes, we could!
We could deliver more than the demand
But this would not happen here



Question: Why won’t we transport more than the demand?



Due to the associated costs!

text:

questions?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Description
Unfortunately, the margins on solar panels are low. After the previous contract has been fulfilled, the company will produce the same number of panels as before. In addition, all three customers want to order the same number of truckloads with solar panels again. The revenue per truckload of panels is 11,000 Euros. The complete production of a truckload of solar panels, including materials, costs 6,300 Euros.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
New Objective
In the new contract, the company wants to maximize its profits while the demand does not have to be fulfilled.

Question: What changes are necessary?



We need to change the objective function
We need to change some parameters
We need to adjust some constraints



Question: Does our decision variable change?



No, we still transport truckloads of solar panels

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
New Parameters
\[
\begin{aligned}
r &: \text{Revenue per truckload of solar panels,} \\
k &: \text{Production costs per truckload of solar panels.}
\end{aligned}
\]







We use \(k\) here, as \(c_{i,j}\) already stands for the transport costs!





Question: What is the profit per truckload of solar panels?


\[
p = r - k
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Former Model
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Minimize} \quad F &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j} \\
\text{subject to:} \quad
&\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad &&\forall j \in \mathcal{J} \\
&X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]

Question: What do we need to change here?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Who Receives No Panels?
Question: One customer will not receive a single panel. Who and why?


The profit per truckload is \(p = 11000 - 6300 = 4700\) Euro
Dresden → Hamburg: \(4700 - 5010 = -310\) Euro
Laupheim → Hamburg: \(4700 - 7120 = -2420\) Euro




Serving Hamburg loses money on both routes!
This is exactly why the demand constraint had to become \(\leq\)

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
The Optimal Profit Plan



Route
Truckloads
Profit




Dresden → Berlin
29
78,880


Laupheim → Munich
17
50,830


→ Hamburg
0
0



The maximal profit is 129,710 Euro.







With the former \(=\) demand constraint, the model would be forced into the unprofitable deliveries to Hamburg!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Model Reflection
Take a moment to think about what we just built:

ComplexityScalabilityAssumptionsVariationsIntegrality


How many decision variables does this problem have?

\(|\mathcal{I}| \times |\mathcal{J}| = 2 \times 3 = 6\) variables
Each represents a shipping route from a production site to a customer.



What happens if we add more production sites?

The number of variables grows as \(|\mathcal{I}| \times |\mathcal{J}|\)

5 sites × 10 customers = 50 variables
10 sites × 20 customers = 200 variables
The model structure stays the same, but computational complexity increases!




What real-world factors are we ignoring?


Vehicle capacity limits per route
Time windows for delivery
Driver working hours and breaks
Traffic conditions and travel time
Fuel costs vs. distance relationship
Possibility of multi-stop routes




How would the model change for different scenarios?


Air transport: Higher costs, faster delivery, weight limits
Multiple vehicle types: Different capacities and costs
Time-sensitive deliveries: Add scheduling constraints




\(X_{i,j} \geq 0\) also allows fractional truckloads. Is that a problem?


Not here: with whole-numbered supplies and demands, this transport problem always has an optimal solution in whole truckloads
This is a special property — most models need extra integrality constraints, e.g., \(X_{i,j} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\)
More on this later in the course!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What Did We Learn?


Modeling Process:

Define the problem clearly
Identify decision variables
Formulate obj. function
Add necessary constraints
Verify completeness


Key Insights:

Sets organize our indices
Parameters hold data
Variables = decisions
Constraints limit feasibility
Obj. drives optimization









This systematic approach works for any optimization problem!

What is algebraic modeling?

Sets
Parameters

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Linear Optimization Model



Basic Model Formulation
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Maximize} \quad F = \sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}} c_j \times X_j
\end{aligned}
\]
subject to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}} a_{i,j} \times X_j  \le b_i && \forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&X_j \ge 0 &&  \forall  j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]



Model Components
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{I} &: \text{set of resources, indexed by } i,\\
\mathcal{J} &: \text{set of activities, indexed by } j,\\
F   &: \text{Objective function variable,}\\
X_{j}   &: \text{decision variables,}\\
c_{j}   &: \text{objective function coefficients,}\\
a_{i,j} &: \text{parameters,}\\
b_{i}   &: \text{parameters}
\end{aligned}
\]



. . .
Question: Have you ever seen something like this before?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What is this good for?

Good Question! A lot of things:

Modeling real-world problems
Solving complex systems
Optimizing resource allocation
Decision-making under constraints
Simulation and prediction

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
From Abstract to Concrete
We’ve just seen the general structure:

Sets (\(\mathcal{I}\), \(\mathcal{J}\))
Parameters (\(c_j\), \(a_{i,j}\), \(b_i\))
Decision variables (\(X_j\))
Objective function and constraints

. . .
Now let’s see how this works with a real problem!
. . .






Watch for these components as we build our first model together.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Description
A company is producing solar panels in Dresden and Laupheim and has to transport them to new solar farms near Hamburg, Munich, and Berlin. The quantities offered and demanded (truckloads) and the transport costs per truckload in Euro are summarized in the following table.

Example: A truckload from Dresden \(i=1\) to Munich \(j=2\) costs \(c_{1,2}=4640\) Euro. Moreover, it is necessary to fulfil all customer demands, as the contract has been signed.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text: Graphical Illustration

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What are we trying?
First, we always need to understand the objectives.
. . .
Question: What are our possible objectives?
Minimizing the transport costs over all truckloads while meeting the demand within the available supply.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Let’s break it down
step by step!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Sets
Remember, sets are collections of elements
. . .
Question: What sets are needed?
. . .
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{I} &: \text{Set of production sites, indexed by } i \text{ with } i \in \{1, \ldots, |\mathcal{I}|\}, \\
\mathcal{J} &: \text{Set of customers, indexed by } j \text{ with } j \in \{1, \ldots, |\mathcal{J}|\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
. . .






We often use plural names for sets and a calligraphic letter, e.g., \(\mathcal{I}\) and \(\mathcal{J}\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Parameters
Parameters are fixed values that are given.
. . .
Question: What parameters are needed?
. . .
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{i,j} &: \text{Costs per truck load for transport from } i \text{ to } j, \\
a_i &: \text{Available truck loads at } i, \\
b_j &: \text{Customer demands at } j.
\end{aligned}
\]
. . .






We usually use the corresponding lower-case letter, e.g., \(c\), \(a\), and \(b\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Decision Variable

Decision variables are the values we are trying to find
Here, our objective is to minimize the transport costs

. . .
Question: What decision variables are needed?
. . .
\[
X_{i,j} : \text{Trucks that deliver panels from site } i \text{ to customer } j.
\]
. . .






We use upper-case letters to distinguish variables from parameters, e.g., \(X\).

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
These are our
building blocks!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Objective Function

The objective function is the value we are trying to minimize (or maximize)
Formalized as a sum of decision variables and parameters

. . .
Question: Do you remember the objective?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Minimizing the Transport Costs
Minimize the transport costs over all truckloads while meeting customer demand within the available supply from production sites.
. . .
Question: How can we write this down?
. . .
\[
\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Constraints

Constraints are conditions that must be met
They limit the solution space!

Question: Objective value without the supply and demand constraints?
. . .

The value is zero
Cheapest option: we simply transport nothing at all!

. . .
Question: What constraints are needed?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Supply Constraints
Ensure that the number of panels transported from a location does not exceed the available panels.
. . .
Question: How can we formalize this?
. . .
\[
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Demand Constraints
Ensure that the demand of each customer is covered.
. . .
Question: Any ideas?
. . .
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Non-negativity Constraints
Ensure no negative number of truckloads are transported.
. . .
Question: Does anyone have an idea how to write this down?
. . .
\[
X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Transport Problem
The complete model can then be written as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Minimize} \quad F &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j} \\
\text{subject to:} \quad
&\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad &&\forall j \in \mathcal{J} \\
&X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Inequality Constraints
Question: Could we replace \(=\) by \(\geq\) in the demand constraint?
. . .

Yes, we could!
We could deliver more than the demand
But this would not happen here

. . .
Question: Why won’t we transport more than the demand?
. . .

Due to the associated costs!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Description
Unfortunately, the margins on solar panels are low. After the previous contract has been fulfilled, the company will produce the same number of panels as before. In addition, all three customers want to order the same number of truckloads with solar panels again. The revenue per truckload of panels is 11,000 Euros. The complete production of a truckload of solar panels, including materials, costs 6,300 Euros.

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
New Objective
In the new contract, the company wants to maximize its profits while the demand does not have to be fulfilled.
. . .
Question: What changes are necessary?
. . .

We need to change the objective function
We need to change some parameters
We need to adjust some constraints

. . .
Question: Does our decision variable change?
. . .

No, we still transport truckloads of solar panels

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
New Parameters
\[
\begin{aligned}
r &: \text{Revenue per truckload of solar panels,} \\
k &: \text{Production costs per truckload of solar panels.}
\end{aligned}
\]
. . .






We use \(k\) here, as \(c_{i,j}\) already stands for the transport costs!



. . .
Question: What is the profit per truckload of solar panels?
. . .
\[
p = r - k
\]

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Former Model
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Minimize} \quad F &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} c_{i,j} \times X_{i,j} \\
\text{subject to:} \quad
&\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} X_{i,j} \leq a_i \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I} \\
&\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} X_{i,j} = b_j \quad &&\forall j \in \mathcal{J} \\
&X_{i,j} \geq 0 \quad &&\forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall j \in \mathcal{J}
\end{aligned}
\]
. . .
Question: What do we need to change here?

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Who Receives No Panels?
Question: One customer will not receive a single panel. Who and why?
. . .

The profit per truckload is \(p = 11000 - 6300 = 4700\) Euro
Dresden → Hamburg: \(4700 - 5010 = -310\) Euro
Laupheim → Hamburg: \(4700 - 7120 = -2420\) Euro

. . .

Serving Hamburg loses money on both routes!
This is exactly why the demand constraint had to become \(\leq\)

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
The Optimal Profit Plan

The maximal profit is 129,710 Euro.
. . .






With the former \(=\) demand constraint, the model would be forced into the unprofitable deliveries to Hamburg!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
Model Reflection
Take a moment to think about what we just built:

ComplexityScalabilityAssumptionsVariationsIntegrality


How many decision variables does this problem have?

\(|\mathcal{I}| \times |\mathcal{J}| = 2 \times 3 = 6\) variables
Each represents a shipping route from a production site to a customer.



What happens if we add more production sites?

The number of variables grows as \(|\mathcal{I}| \times |\mathcal{J}|\)

5 sites × 10 customers = 50 variables
10 sites × 20 customers = 200 variables
The model structure stays the same, but computational complexity increases!




What real-world factors are we ignoring?


Vehicle capacity limits per route
Time windows for delivery
Driver working hours and breaks
Traffic conditions and travel time
Fuel costs vs. distance relationship
Possibility of multi-stop routes




How would the model change for different scenarios?


Air transport: Higher costs, faster delivery, weight limits
Multiple vehicle types: Different capacities and costs
Time-sensitive deliveries: Add scheduling constraints




\(X_{i,j} \geq 0\) also allows fractional truckloads. Is that a problem?


Not here: with whole-numbered supplies and demands, this transport problem always has an optimal solution in whole truckloads
This is a special property — most models need extra integrality constraints, e.g., \(X_{i,j} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\)
More on this later in the course!

title: Lecture I - Welcome and Introduction
text:
What Did We Learn?


Modeling Process:

Define the problem clearly
Identify decision variables
Formulate obj. function
Add necessary constraints
Verify completeness


Key Insights:

Sets organize our indices
Parameters hold data
Variables = decisions
Constraints limit feasibility
Obj. drives optimization



. . .






This systematic approach works for any optimization problem!
